newsitem.title: USA: DuPont loses appeal against pollution insurers.
newsitem.headline: DuPont loses appeal against pollution insurers.

text.p: The Delaware Supreme Court ruled on Wednesday that the DuPont Co and not its insurers must pay for toxic waste cleanups on company property, court papers said.

The ruling upheld a lower court decision in a lawsuit filed in 1989 by DuPont to recover hundreds of millions of dollars from insurers in cleanup costs for 14 sites. The ruling also denied DuPont reimbursement of cleanup costs for off-site pollution unless it is done as a result of a court or government order.

An attorney for one of the defendants, Travelers Group unit Travelers Indemnity Co, Robert Cusumano, told Reuters "The court has done two things in this decision. First, it has imposed upon manufacturers an obligation to prevent pollution from spreading; and second, it has said that insurance does not cover the cost of cleaning up your own property."

To make the case more manageable, the Delaware lower court selected three "illustrative" sites for trial, two in New York and one in New Jersey. DuPont sought reimbursement for $36 million in cleanup costs from Travelers, Allstate Insurance Co and several other insurers.
"Although the court's decision focuses on three particular sites, its holding will certainly affect all the cleanup costs at issue in the entire case", Cusumano said.

"For the first time a state Supreme Court has looked at the question of insurance coverage for a manufacturer's own property and dealt with it in a manner that looks at all the issues...We think it will be very persuasive to courts around the country", Cusumano said.

DuPont spokeswoman Catherine Andriadis told Reuters, "Although we are disappointed in the ruling, the court did not preclude insurance coverage for groundwater remediation. So for duPont this was a mixed result. We will continue to clean up our sites regardless of whether the court requires the insurance companies to pay a share."

DuPont associate general counsel John Klocko told Reuters "our reading" is that under New York and New Jersey law, groundwater is considered public property and therefore covered by insurance policies.

"This ruling has absolutely no effect on DuPont's bottom line because we have spent hundreds of millions of dollars cleaning up environmental contamination on our plant sites and off. All we're trying to do here is have insurance companies pay part of our costs", Klocko said.
